speechtext:
Hon. members will allow me, I am sure, to point out to them that today is the birthday anniversary of the dean of our house, the hon. member for Fort William. I want to tell him how pleased we are to see him looking so young and full of activity. We wish him very many happy returns of the day.
Whereupon the members of the house sang Happy Birthday to You.

quite tickled at hearing your words, Mr. Speaker, and especially at the fine music that has come from the house. I enjoy living very much, and I am going to carry on as long as a wise Providence permits and my better half helps.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF SCRAPIE DISEASE IN ALBERTA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Can the minister tell the house in what part of Alberta the disease scrapie has broken out? Are there any other parts of Canada where this disease has broken out? How many sheep have been condemned for slaughter in Alberta and in other parts of Canada? What compensation, if any, does the government intend paying for each slaughtered head?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF SCRAPIE DISEASE IN ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question asks in what part of Alberta the disease scrapie has broken out, and whether there are other parts of Canada in which it has broken out.
The use of the term "broken out" in connection with scrapie conveys a wrong implication. This is not a highly infectious disease which spreads rapidly from flock to flock, as do such diseases as hog cholera and foot-and-mouth disease. It is believed to be transmitted to some extent by breeding, but much research is still required to determine its exact mode of transmission.
Although it has been known to exist for some time in Europe and Great Britain, it is relatively rare on this continent; and in both United States and Canada the practice is followed of slaughtering infected flocks, with compensation, as a general safeguard and protection to the sheep industry.
Scrapie was recently diagnosed in one flock of sheep in Alberta, and at the present time that flock is in the process of being ordered

Inquiries of the Ministry slaughtered and arrangements made for compensation. In the meantime, the flock is quarantined. Pending completion of arrangements it is not considered desirable to release details, but such details will be made available, if desired, when the disposal operations have been completed.
Scrapie has not yet been diagnosed in any other flock of sheep in Canada since 1954. It was first diagnosed in Canada in 1945 in an Ontario flock. Since that date, and not including the present instance in Alberta, it has been diagnosed in five flocks, all in Ontario. In each case the infected flock was destroyed. The total number of animals involved in all five flocks was 287.
The general plan that is followed in such cases will be followed in Alberta.

subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF SCRAPIE DISEASE IN ALBERTA
speechtext: What was the compensation paid in Ontario when those sheep were slaughtered?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF SCRAPIE DISEASE IN ALBERTA
speechtext: It is worked out on that basis. As far as the present herd is concerned the owner has suggested a certain compensation. We have had the herd inspected and we have proposed a certain compensation. The matter is still under discussion.

subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF SCRAPIE DISEASE IN ALBERTA
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? In the latter part of my question I asked the minister what compensation had been paid in 1954 to the Ontario people? Do I understand that the herd has not been paid for yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF SCRAPIE DISEASE IN ALBERTA
speechtext: No. That has been taken care of. The total number of animals involved in all five flocks was 287, but I have not the amount.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the stage of this legislation when we are supposed to discuss the general principle of the bill. There are many, of course, who would say that as far as this

bill is concerned there is no principle. However, such as it is, the principle is contained in the title of the bill, which reads:
An act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
In other words, this is an expedient to put a limited amount of cash into the hands of a limited number of farmers who have been unable to secure that cash in the normal way by the sale of their grain. The very wording of the title demonstrates the failure of the government to realize the seriousness of the cash situation of the prairie grain grower. To begin with, the bill says, "to meet temporary financial difficulties." The situation, I think, cannot properly be called temporary.
The minister is capable of taking a very liberal view, I know, of what the meaning of the word "temporary" may be, but I would submit that this shortage of cash on the part of western grain growers has been getting progressively worse over the past three years. This is not something that has come up only this year; it has been with us now for some considerable time. Moreover, the situation is steadily growing worse.
When you look at all the factors concerned, I think you will realize there is very little real prospect of this situation coming to an end in the next few months or in the limited period of one year that this bill is provided to cover. We have a very large surplus of grain, both stored in the elevators and still on the farms. The United States also has a very large carryover of grain. The general world wheat situation is one of surplus supply. Under those circumstances I do not think there is any real possibility of the present shortage of cash in the hands of the wheat farmers being really relieved for a period of at least two or three years in the future.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government stubbornly refuse to admit that this is the situation. The minister at every opportunity talks of the improved sales position and comes out with optimistic statements, thereby attempting to spread the general idea that soon the farmer will be able to get rid of his grain and his cash difficulties will be at an end. I think that is merely raising false hopes. Instead of engaging in talk of that sort the minister should be addressing himself to some more realistic and definite means of solving the general difficulties brought about by the inability to sell our surplus grain and the resulting serious cash position of western farmers.
Grain
The full title of the bill continues with these words:
... to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
I emphasize the word "all". From reading this one would think that the farmers have been able to deliver a large proportion of their grain, but let us look at the actual situation. As far as last year's crop is concerned, a considerable number of farmers have only been able to deliver 300 bushels of wheat or 500 bushels of barley or 800 bushels of oats, enough in any event to give the farmer around $300 or at the most $350. This amount is quite insufficient to meet even his harvesting expenses, let alone any of his other expenses.
In addition, a one-bushel quota has been provided at a certain number of points in western Canada, and I believe a two-bushel quota was provided at a limited number of points. However, the fact that a quota is established, no matter what it is, does not mean that the farmer has been able to deliver that much grain. An eight-bushel quota was established with respect to last year's crop, but a considerable number of people were not able to deliver the eight bushel quota. They were still delivering on the eight bushel quota after they had harvested their last crop. In effect the situation is that as far as last year's crop is concerned the farmers in some cases have been able to deliver no grain and in other cases only a limited amount. Therefore when the bill refers to inability to deliver all their grain I think it gives a false impression.
When the legislation was discussed at the resolution stage the position of this party was made very clear. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), I and others made very clear what we thought of the legislation. Our view can be summed up in four words. We did not like it. We did not like it at the resolution stage and we do not like it now that it has reached the second reading stage. We believe the measure is totally inadequate to meet the situation existing in western Canada brought about by a lack of cash, and that a much better method to deal with the situation is available in the form of cash advances on farm-stored grain.
The three general grounds on which this particular proposal has been attacked in the house were argued very extensively at the resolution stage by many members on this side, and I do not propose to repeat all the arguments put forward then in order to show that this was a completely inadequate and

Grain
poor piece of legislation. I will merely summarize them. The first general ground of complaint with the legislation is that the maximum amount that can be lent, $1,500, is insufficient so far as a large number of farmers are concerned. We have also been told that the average amount of the loans actually made so far is in the neighbourhood of $800.
I think it is quite clear that $800, or $1,500 in the case of a larger farm, is totally inadequate to meet the farmer's harvesting expenses, pay his taxes, provide him with food, fuel and clothing to carry him through the winter, and take care of the various other expenses he has to meet.
For that reason alone the legislation is unsatisfactory. It does not do the job which it says it is going to do. It does not provide enough funds for the majority of the people who may want to take advantage of it.
The second general ground of complaint on this bill is that the interest rate of 5 per cent is not justified. The loans are government guaranteed, and as everyone knows the rate of interest on government bonds, for example, is 3 per cent. The rate of interest on other loans guaranteed by the government is 3 per cent or 3| per cent. Under these circumstances the farmers cannot understand why a rate of 5 per cent is justified. One might say that the risk to the bank is negligible.
Apart altogether from the interest rate, which is unsatisfactory, the farmer in western Canada does not believe he should pay interest on this money at all. He looks upon the payment of interest, as has been pointed out, as a payment of interest on his last years' wages. He looks upon it as very inequitable that he should be called upon to pay this toll on what he has already earned.
The third general complaint in regard to this bill is that many farmers cannot get loans under it. The very men who perhaps need the cash worst are the ones to whom the bank is unwilling to make advances. In addition to that, as has been pointed out also, a very large number of farmers do not deal with banks. In some cases they live 40 or 50 miles away from banks. The banker does not know them, and therefore is not prepared to make loans. One might sum up all of these objections to this legislation by saying it just does not meet the situation and is not what the farmers have requested.
On the other hand, we should consider a system of cash advances, which is what the farmers desire and what the organizations who have spoken for the farmers have requested. We find that all the arguments
[Mr. Harkness.l
which can be put forward against the proposed legislation do not apply to a system of cash advances. The argument put forward by the minister and other members of his party against cash advances is that such a system would make the wheat board into a lending institution, and that the wheat board has not the staff to handle cash advances. It is said it would be impossible for the board to look after a system of that sort.
I feel that both these arguments were completely shattered by the discussion we had during the resolution stage of this bill. I believe it is quite apparent to anyone that a cash advance is not a loan. There is a distinct difference, for example, between going to a farmer and putting down $10 on a cow which he is to deliver a month later, and going out and lending him $10. The farmer understands that. The livestock business used to be conducted on that basis. You went out and bought stock, and put so much down on it. Essentially that is what is being asked for so far as the system of cash advances is concerned. It is really a payment on account, which is a different thing from a loan as the minister tried to represent it. The argument, therefore, that making these payments on account to farmers for grain stored in their granaries would put the wheat board in the same class as a lending institution, or convert, it into a banking institution, just does not hold up.
The other argument, from the mechanical point of view, that the wheat board is not set up to handle a scheme of this sort, that it has not the staff, is equally without any strength. Ever since its inception the wheat board has been making advances to farmers. The advances were in the form of initial payments when the farmers delivered grain to the elevators.
There is no essential difference between making a payment of that sort and making a payment on grain while it is still stored in the farmer's bin. There may be a little more risk, but I am not arguing that particular point. Even so, I would maintain that the amount of risk is negligible. The risk in that case is that when this payment is entered in the farmer's permit book, he is then in a position where he cannot deliver any more grain unless this is taken account of, and his opportunities for selling grain except to the wheat board are extremely limited. In most cases they are nil. His only other customers are neighbours who may buy grain for feed. Most farmers already have more grain than they can feed, so he has practically no market. In some cases there is a little exchange of grain going on with implement dealers and other appliance dealers.

However, in effect the farmer has only the one customer and that is the wheat board.
I think there is no question but that as the wheat board, an agency of the government, is the farmer's only customer, the government has the responsibility for making cash advances to the farmer so he can pay his normal expenses. We in this party believe that a system of cash advances would be a much better method of handling the situation than this legislation which has been presented to us and which we believe to be completely inadequate for the purpose.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale):
That Bill No. 82 be not now read the second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the Introduction of legislation which will provide for cash payments on farm-stored grain.
Before I sit down there is one other matter I should like to mention and that is the attitude which the minister took during the previous debate and which I think is open to serious question. He made what was nothing less than a threat to the members of this house. He said, in effect, that if we did not stop discussing this piece of legislation, which had been under discussion only a short time, he would withdraw it until the end of the session. The implication was that he would leave the farmers in a position where they could not get loans of any sort, and the responsibility would be ours.
I am fairly certain the minister will not try to carry out that threat because every farmer in this country would know that the responsibility was the minister's. This minister, and the government which supports him, would be responsible if the farmers could not get more loans. The members of the opposition would not be responsible merely because they had made proper criticism of the legislation the minister proposed, and were going on the theory that it might be possible to get the government to reconsider this legislation and bring in something better.
I would say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that threats of that sort serve the exactly opposite purpose to that which the minister intended. That sort of disregard for parliament is the very sort of thing which makes all of us determined not to obey what amounts tQ a piece of dictation, a threat, or whatever you would like to call it.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather unusual to see our friends in the official opposition make an about-face which is so obvious, because it was at the resolution stage of this legislation that they said there were enough good

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I interpret the amendment moved by the hon. member it is to the effect that the bill be not now read a second time. To me it indicates a position that the members of the official opposition did not take at the resolution stage.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We did not have the bill then. How could we?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member could have voted against the resolution, as we did. We voted against it, as my leader pointed out, so we would not in any way indicate our support for this half measure which might prevent the introduction of legislation which would do some good, and which is really wanted. We wanted legislation in the line of a continuation of orderly marketing through cash advances on farm-stored grain, as was advocated by this group in the amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
The title of the bill before the house is an indication of the deceit in the bill. It is an act to provide short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain. It is an act to provide short-term credit to grain producers and, Mr. Speaker, it has failed miserably in this regard because, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out, only around 8,000 farmers in the three prairie provinces have seen fit to, or were able to, obtain a loan under the provisions of this legislation out of the 200,000 farmers or thereabouts who are in western Canada.

Grain
It has also failed, Mr. Speaker, because the average loan taken out is around $800, which is a little over half of $1,500, which the legislation was heralded as providing to western farmers. It is deceitful in this regard because it does not provide for nor live up to the expectations of western farmers. I have a question on the order paper requesting a breakdown on the number and size of the loans, but evidently the minister does not want the question to be answered until this stage of the debate has passed, because on page 980 of Hansard the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
I will give the hon. member the information now if he wants it.
It is now nearly one week later, and the question is still unanswered. That can only be interpreted as an effort on the part of the government to cover up some of the bad features of this legislation, to cover up the dismal failure which it has been.
The legislation was bound to fail, Mr. Speaker. There are 1,200 shipping points in Saskatchewan, but at the same time there are only 159 points served by 257 branch banks. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce well knows, the distances in the western prairies are great and the legislation is just not adaptable to those circumstances. It is very difficult for the farmer to go 50 or 60 miles to get a loan from a branch bank he has never visited before and where he is unknown. It has been pointed out in previous speeches that unless the banker is in a position to have complete confidence in the borrower, he is not going to make the loan.
The legislation was bound to fail because of the red tape which was attached to its application. The first form brought out dealing with applications for loans, the form that the farmer would fill out after he had travelled 50 miles to visit a branch bank, required him to put down everything except the money in the kiddy's piggy bank. It asked for a net worth statement on behalf of the bank; liens that were against the grain; the amount of grain that he would have a chance to market in his own right; the amount of grain the landlord would be entitled to. It made him list any chattel liens against the grain. That is an indication of the attitude of the government in bringing down legislation that has so much red tape attached to it that we could not expect the farmer to fill out the form to get the loan and return and get his $1,500.
We must give a great deal of credit to the members of the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the officials of that organization who, realizing that their battle for cash advances

on farm-stored grain was perhaps useless in the face of government inactivity, met with the officials of the Department of Finance and had this form amended to take some of the sting out of it and make it a little easier for farmers to get loans. But still on the form there is a certificate by the responsible banker indicating his confidence in the reliability of the farmer. In other words if there is any risk involved the bank manager will not make the loan.
I say this legislation was bound to fail, as the hon. member for Calgary North pointed out, because of the 5 per cent interest rate involved. The Minister of Trade and Commerce added it all up and came up with a figure of around $20. I do not think that is the point. The principle of the legislation is what bothers the farmers in western Canada. They do not forget the depression they went through. They do not forget how often a little bit of debt can mushroom and pyramid and eventually break them. Therefore they are very reluctant indeed to take on further debt based on their own earning capacity.
We must also take into consideration the relationship of the farmers to the small businessmen and merchants in town to indicate again why this legislation was bound to fail. If I, as an individual farmer, owe $500 to the implement dealer in my town, I would be in no rush to pay it by means of this loan if I wanted to be a good businessman. If I did not have the money I would not go and borrow money at 5 per cent interest to pay a debt which was in effect costing me nothing. The businessman is going to sell me machines in the future. Therefore I am not going to incur a debt of 5 per cent to pay off a debt which through his good graces is not costing me anything. It is not that the businessman would not like to charge some interest but he realizes the people he is going to have to deal with in the future, through thick and thin, are these same farmers.
The grocer is in the same position, and the oil dealer. We can see the unfairness of this legislation and the hardship it works on these small merchants, the implement dealers and the independent grocers, in carrying the debts of the farmers. There is no alternative; the farmers are forced to borrow money on their own earnings at 5 per cent if they are to pay them off.
The alternative, of course, to this whole proposal, as was pointed out by my leader, is cash advances for farm-stored grain, a system whereby the farmer would be entitled as a right to some return for the product he has produced in the year and which he now cannot sell.

I think the various aspects of the operation of a cash advance on farm-stored grain have been fairly well spelled out, but they have fallen on many ignorant ears. The Minister of Trade and Commerce indicates his objection to cash advances on farm-stored grain, as reported at page 128 of Hansard:
You must be careful about lending on grain where only limited security can be had. The grain on the farm would be the only security the board would have.
In effect the minister has said that you cannot trust the western farmer. He goes on to point out that as circumstances present themselves, farmers might feed their grain to their hogs or sell it to a neighbour. I wonder what has caused such a reverse in the minister's attitude toward the western farmer, because in 1951 when discussing a similar piece of legislation that was before us he outlined that the interest rate could be 5 per cent and he said, as reported at page 2034 of Hansard:
The basis for my opinion that the government's liability under its guarantee is negligible rests fundamentally upon my belief in the integrity and good faith of western grain growers.
That is rather an about-face in five years. In one case the minister says you can charge a low interest rate. I am assuming that the minister at that time thought 5 per cent was a low interest rate. He said you could do this because of the integrity of western farmers; but he now says you cannot make cash advances on farm-stored grain because the farmers will spirit it away in the night and the losses will be excessive.
Tbe second phase of the bill, Mr. Speaker, as it states, is to meet temporary financial difficulties. This is just another case of more deceit. Certainly these conditions have not just popped up overnight. They did not just develop on November 15, 1955. The agricultural share of the national income has been declining continuously for the last five years. According to the Canadian Journal of Agricultural Economics, volume 3, No. 2, we find that in 1954 the farmers of Canada received the lowest share of the national income they have ever received in my lifetime. They received 6-8 per cent of the national income as opposed to the other low period of 6-9 per cent in 1931.
When we consider that agriculture involves approximately 20 per cent of the population of Canada we are indeed being deceitful when we say this is a temporary financial situation. This is the financial position of the farmer as related to other aspects of the agricultural picture. We cannot say it is just the price of wheat, because it is related to these other matters which have been brought up in
Grain
debate. It is related to the fact that there is no floor price on hogs and there is no realistic floor price on eggs. When you have circumstances where farmers in western Canada are receiving 28 cents a dozen for eggs and 25 cents less than the floor price for hogs and a drop in the price of beef, you are able to make a more complete appraisal of this temporary financial difficulty, as it is termed in the bill.
Of course the farmers all over Canada are suffering from the price-cost squeeze, which is perhaps more pointed in the case of western Canadian farmers because as is generally realized, the occupation of the grain grower is more precarious and hazardous than for other mixed forms of agriculture. It is more sensitive to the rises and falls in our economy. In relation to the price-cost squeeze there is a general movement on behalf of the farm organizations to try and correct it.
I do not think the way to bring the level of farm income up is to bring the income of the other organizations down; but my colleague the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) certainly indicated one way this squeeze could be curbed. He indicated that there was a refusal on the part of the government to make a deal with the government of Poland whereby we could get cement in return for wheat. In fact it was even more favourable to the government than that; we would have to buy a certain amount of cement from the Polish government, and they in turn would buy a much larger amount of wheat from us. This of course will meet with the general approval of western farmers who have to buy United States cement at $2.65 a bag because they cannot get Canadian cement. They pay 80 cents a bag more for cement because of the failure of this government to carry out some policy which would provide them with cement on the one hand and sell our wheat on the other.
The bill goes on to state that it is designed to provide short-term credit to meet the temporary financial difficulty of the western farmers arising from their inability to deliver all their grain. What an insult to western farmers to indicate that they are in financial difficulties because they cannot deliver all their grain. Far from being able to deliver all their grain as of January 25, we have delivered in grain marketings from the farm slightly over half as much as the average in the preceding ten year period. This is an indication to me that we have not been able to deliver even a fraction of all our grain. We have delivered 75 million bushels less than last year at this time.
I think in fairness the government could do very well to expunge that whole title from

Grain
the bill and put one in that would be more suitable to the desire and wishes of western farmers. Not only is it because of our inability to market all our grain or even a small portion of it that we are in financial difficulties; it is because of the gross inequality in the opportunities to deliver. The whole situation of box car allocation and distribution has been a most vexing one in western Canada.
I received a letter from the secretary of the wheat pool committee at Mendham, in that same area the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to in answer to my question on the orders of the day. I shall read it, because it certainly gives an appreciation of the circumstances that affect farmers in that area. The letter is addressed to me:
Dear Sir:
A very serious situation is facing the farmers and business people of this district.
Mr. Gardiner made a statement that more money has been paid out to farmers since August 1 than over the same period last year. This is not so in our district and neighbouring points.
Since August 1 the average income of farmers here has been approximately $350. Thanks to the business firms which have been able to carry the burden till now. But there is a climax to all.
Since August 1 we are short 70 box cars compared to the same period last year, besides the fact that a number of the 90 cars received this year was used to fill the 8 bushel quota of the previous year. The situation was serious then. How serious is it now?
In comparison to the grain that has been moved from the prairies since August 1 where does the proportion of the grain of the Mendham district come in?
We farmers hereby request that immediate action be taken so we get more box cars.
Yours very truly,
Bernard Zubot,
Secretary of
Mendham pool committee.

speechtext: Before making any comment may I ask upon what citation or ruling you based the first part of your remarks, with respect to the relevancy of the amendment to the bill now under consideration?

speechtext:
Citation 662 reads:
The principle of relevancy in an amendment governs every proposed resolution, which, on the second reading of a bill, must not include in its scope other bills then standing for consideration by the house. Nor may such an amendment deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee, not attach conditions to the second reading of the bill.
I gave as an example the distinction which could be made between housing and rental because I thought the house would remember that that case was before Mr. Speaker Macdonald a few years ago, and that was his decision.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I based my amendment on the authority of Beauchesne's second edition, paragraph 755, to be found at page 217, which reads:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction-
The rest of the paragraph is not applicable. I do not think there is any question but that this amendment is declaratory of some principle adverse to or differing from the principles, policies or provisions of the bill. As you have pointed out yourself, the bill provides for loans and the amendment provides

Grain
that the bill shall be withdrawn and that there shall be substituted legislation to provide for cash payments on farm-stored grain.
As I read this particular section of Beau-chesne I would think it would be quite in order to introduce an amendment of that sort. I find that there are a number of precedents for amendments of this kind. At page 1136 of Hansard of March 27, 1950, will be found an amendment of a similar type. That amendment dealt with Bill No. 16, to amend the agricultural products act, and read as follows:
That Bill No. 16 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introducing of a permanent agricultural products export act which would provide for the setting up of an export board, to fill present contracts, negotiate future contracts, and develop new markets abroad for surplus agricultural products.
Representations were made in connection with the amendment and it was allowed. On the same day another amendment of the same type was introduced, to be found at page 1157. This was in connection with Bill No. 17 to amend the Agricultural Prices Support Act. The amendment provided that floor prices should be established at such levels as to guarantee to producers a price-cost relationship.
Then on Wednesday, March 29, an amendment was moved which was really on all fours with this one. That will be found at page 1368 of Hansard for that date. The house was dealing with Bill No. 54 to amend the Fisheries Prices Support Act and the amendment moved read as follows:
That Bill No. 54 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introducing of legislation to amend the Fisheries Prices Support Act so as to provide that floor prices should be established at such levels as to guarantee to those engaged in the fishing industry a price-cost relationship not less favourable than that prevailing in the period 1944-48.
In view of section 755 of Beauchesne and these precedents I did not consider that there would be any question of this amendment not being in order.

speechtext:
On a point of order, as I understand it, it is suggested that the amendment might be out of order on one or both of two grounds; first, that it is not relevant to the bill now before us; and second, that it deals with a matter upon which the opinion of the house has already been taken. May I deal with those two points in that order?
I submit that my colleague the hon. member for Calgary North has effectively dealt with the question of the propriety of the amendment standing on its own, that is apart from the question of whether it repeats the amendment previously offered. But I would like to suggest, in addition to what he has said, that citation 662, which Your Honour was kind enough to refer me to in answer to my question, does not seem to be applicable under the circumstances. It reads:
The principle of relevancy in an amendment governs every proposed resolution, which, on the second reading of a bill, must not include in its scope other bills then standing for consideration by the house.
I hardly see how this amendment could be said to include in its scope any other bill standing for consideration. The citation goes on:
Nor may such an amendment deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved-
Still it does not deal with the detailed provisions of the bill upon which it is moved. It suggests an alternative principle, an entirely different alternative, or rather an alternative not related to the detailed provisions of the bill. It asserts a contrary principle, and I make that statement without any

Grain
hesitation. It asserts a contrary principle without the adoption of which the hon. member moving the amendment could not agree to the bill. Then the citation continues:
-nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee, nor attach conditions to the second reading of the bill.
I submit it is quite obvious that it does neither of those. Your Honour referred to the question of relevancy, and we may as well deal with all the points that have been raised. I wonder if the hon. member may have had in mind citation 657, which is the same as the citation already read by the hon. member for Calgary North from Beauchesne's second edition. This is exactly what is being done here. The hon. member is placing on record a special reason for not agreeing to the second reading of the bill, and is therefore moving a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill. He is thus advancing a different proposition, but it is still relevant because both the amendment and the bill itself deal with the same general subject. Your Honour, I think, distinguished them on the basis that the amendment deals with cash advances whereas you said the bill deals with short-term credit. I think you are placing an entirely too restrictive interpretation on the bill. May I read the short title?
This act may be cited as the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, 1956.
It says "interim financing". The bill deals with the subject of placing cash in the hands of prairie farmers because of an emergency situation that has arisen.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would suggest that the general principle or purpose of the bill is to place cash in the hands of prairie farmers which they require because of an emergency. The method by which that is to be done is dealt with under the detailed provisions of the

bill, and the bill proposes in its detailed provisions to do it by guaranteeing loans through banks, but the purpose or principle is to place cash in the hands of prairie farmers.
My hon. friend from Calgary North says we propose to the house that the same purpose and principle be achieved, that is, that cash be placed in the hands of prairie farmers, but by another detailed method, namely by requiring the wheat board to make cash advances. So the principle of the two proposals is identical, and that, I submit to you, is proven conclusively by reference to the short title, "Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act". The purpose is to enable the interim financing of prairie producers. One proposes in detail to do it through guaranteed bank loans; the other proposes to do it through cash advances by the wheat board. The amendment is most certainly relevant to the principle of the bill. It seeks to advance the same purpose as the bill seeks to achieve, only by a different and much more acceptable method.
I should have thought that Your Honour- and I make the suggestion with deference- probably attaches more weight to the proposition that this amendment has been anticipated by the amendment moved earlier by the C.C.F. party. I should like, then, to deal with that proposition. Here I think I should be able to convince you that the two amendments are different. The amendment moved by the C.C.F., which is to be found on page 53 of Hansard, proposed to add to the amendment moved by my leader on that occasion the following words:
-including their failure to provide cash advances on farm-stored grain, equal to not less than 75 per cent of the initial price, to alleviate the serious financial crisis now confronting western farmers and the entire economy of the prairie provinces.
The purpose and principle of that amendment was to condemn the government for not having done something. That was the sole object of that amendment. It was a motion of censure upon the government for their failure to do something, whereas the amendment now before us proposes, by way of a positive amendment, that the government, instead of proceeding by way of guaranteed loans, should proceed by way of cash advances. So I submit to you that to move censure of the government for its failure to do something is not the same as advancing in a substantive motion that another principle be substituted for the principle of the bill now before us.
I agree that it would be the same thing if we moved, say on a motion to go into supply, an amendment to censure the government for not having made cash advances. Then we

Grain
would be clearly repeating the previous motion, a motion censuring the government for failure to do something. But when the amendment before us moves that a bill be not now read a second time but that instead the house resolve that cash advances should be made, that is to my mind something quite different from a motion of non-confidence in the government condemning it for its failure, and a detailed failure; that is, a failure to provide cash advances equal to not less than 75 per cent of the initial price.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member, just to ask him this. If the two motions-the one that was moved by way of a subamendment to the address in reply, and this one to the second reading of the bill-are in fact two motions on which the judgment of the house is required, would they then be regarded as the same if it were not for the fact that the hon. member contends that there is distinction between a motion of censure and a motion that is an amendment to the second reading of the bill?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think I have stated it as clearly as I can. To censure the government on one occasion, before any legislation has been introduced, for their failure to do a certain thing which is then positively stated, that is, make cash advances equivalent to 75 per cent, is a different thing from saying on this occasion that the bill should not be read a second time now but that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation which will provide for cash payments on farm-stored grain. I do not think I could be making any argument at all if such an amendment had been moved as a vote of censure or nonconfidence on a supply motion, but when a positive alternative is put forward by way of amendment to the motion for second reading of a bill I submit that the one motion has not been anticipated by the other and that there is sufficient difference, if you like, to make this another borderline case upon which you should perhaps reserve your final decision.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Before the hon. member concludes his argument, may I say that I am very much interested in all he has said. Of course he realizes there is the general principle that no two questions substantially the same should be offered to the judgment of the house in the same session. That is the principle, and I would point out to him that by ancient usage the formalities attached to the presentation of an amendment to the motion respecting the address in reply to the speech from the throne involve an addition
to the motion, and that an amendment to the second reading of a bill is made by way of deleting all the words after "that" and inserting other words. These are the formalities as to the method of presenting a motion, but I would submit to the hon. member that they do not alter the principle that two motions substantially the same shall not be offered to the judgment of the house in the same session. He has already agreed that these two are substantially the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rarely intervene in these discussions because I think you set things before us fairly clearly, but for the record I do want to dissent from the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kamloops that if the opposition on the address, on the six supply motions or on the budget cast their reflections on the government in a negative form, they are not then held accountable to the rule of anticipation. That in effect is what he has just said; and if what he has said should happen to become the practice of the house we would have these motions made from the beginning until the end of the session, and none of them precluding similar motions provided they are cast in the positive sense thereafter. 1 do not think even the hon. member for Kamloops seriously recommends that course.
On that point let me say this. In the wording of the subamendment moved by the C.C.F. party it is true that the word "legislation" was not used with respect to cash advances, and it is in the amendment before us; but any amendment or subamendment that may be moved on the address is, in a negative sense, based on the absence of legislation by the government, and the use of the word in itself is not necessary to indicate that what the opposition does mean is that we ought to do something by legislation.

I am basing my remarks today on principles, and I am prepared to state them to the house. The hon. member for Kamloops has doubted the point I made with respect to relevancy. There is no question about relevancy-Perhaps some of these days the house may consider doing for the Speaker of the House of Commons what has been done for the Speaker of the commons of Australia, give him a table which could be removed on ceremonial occasions and replaced during debates during which the Speaker has to refer to many books-I have before me May, fifteenth edition, and at page 508 there is the following:
The principle of relevancy in an amendment governs every such motion.
This is the chapter dealing with the second reading of bills and amendments thereto, and in saying that May refers to page 400 of the same volume where I find the following:
The fundamental rule that debate must be relevant to a question necessarily involves the rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed.
This is why, in order to illustrate my point of view, I indicated to the house the distinction between housing and rental. I remember that when a bill regarding housing was presented in the house either the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre proposed an amendment regarding the control of rentals. It may be that the Speaker of the time did not quite make that point. Perhaps he did not rest his judgment exclusively on that point, but having looked at them I think that this is the best point.
The amendment would switch the discussion from credit to cash advances. Therefore what would we have? We would have a debate which would be a repetition of that which took place on the amendment to the address in reply moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in January.
There is no question as to the second principle, that no two questions substantially the same shall be offered to the house for its judgment in the same session. I would point out to the hon. member for Kamloops that the only difference between an amendment to the second reading of a bill and an amendment to the address in reply which he calls a vote of censure is in the method of presentation, which has been fixed by ancient usage, and which provides that an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne has to be made by way of addition whereas in this case an amendment has to be made differently. Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank you for resolving this point before I had completed my remarks because while I did not have an amendment to move to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Calgary North, I have an amendment that I am going to move which is in a slightly different vein.
The last time I was on my feet I was discussing the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary North. Since it has now been ruled out of order I presume I could have another 40 minutes, but I can assure the house I am not going to take that long.
I was interested to note the tactics used by the official opposition in introducing this amendment. Their tactics were appreciated, because they indicated they are prepared to follow our leadership in fighting the battle for the western farmer to achieve cash advances on farm-stored grain, and that they will oppose this legislation which is inadequate.
One of the main reasons, Mr. Speaker, for the financial plight of the western farmer is the inefficiency of the transport controller. I have a copy of a resolution from the municipality of Miry Creek, which is south of the Saskatchewan river and in a similar area to the Burstall subdivision referred to in my question this morning. This is a copy of a letter which was sent to the Canadian wheat board and it says:
At the regular meeting of the council of this municipality on the 3rd instant, a resolution was passed to acquaint your board with the unequal distribution of box cars for grain hauling. This discrimination or unequal distribution of box cars having a serious financial effect on those farmers who must utilize the services of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
It has been pointed out that on the north side of the South Saskatchewan river, which is serviced by the Canadian National Railway, there appears to be no shortage of box cars. In fact, the fanners there have filled their 3-bushel quota and we are advised that there is sufficient space available for another 1 bushel quota.

Grain
Generally speaking, the farmers on the empress line of the Canadian Pacific Railway have been able to haul only the original unit of 300 bushels. At present, there is no further room available for additional delivery of wheat should a quota open.
That is signed by G. L. Brace, secretary treasurer of the rural municipality of Miry Creek. It gives us some indication of the failure of the individual charged with the responsibility of seeing that the marketing points in western Canada have an equal opportunity to market grain. [DOT] On November 21 and November 22 when I visited that area I became aware of the inequalities. As I crossed the South Saskatchewan river it became obvious that there was a shortage of space on the Canadian Pacific Railway line. At that time I wired the transport controller from both Sceptre and Richmound, but received no reply. Representations were again made when I came to Ottawa; I tried to communicate with the transport controller but found he was not available. I am asking now, just who is responsible for fulfilling the duties of the transport controller when he is out of town? I presume it is his $50 per week secretary.
One other manifestation of this problem of car allocation is the discrimination against farmers who wish to deliver to the elevator of their choice. In Saskatchewan pool district No. 4 we find that to date, compared with the same period last year, there is an increase in the percentage of wheat shipped from 14 stations by an average of 3-7 per cent, but there is a decrease in the percentage at 19 stations of an average of 5-2 per cent. This is perhaps just another aspect of the problem introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) at page 1009 of Hansard, when he stated:
X grant that one hon. member said yesterday that one of his constituents wrote and told him he had been unable to deliver any grain since the fall of 1954. At the same time he went on to say it was because he could not deliver to the elevator of his choice. Well if the constituent is so independent as to insist on the elevator of his choice, then he cannot be as badly in need of cash as the hon. member would seek to establish.
That is the attitude of government members on the agriculture committee, because they do not appreciate the democratic principle of allowing farmers to deliver to the elevator of their choice. They take the attitude that if it is all right with the United Grain Growers and the line elevator companies, it is all right for the farmers to make them deliver to any elevator in which there is room.
At the same time the hon. member for Kootenay indicated that he was asking this house to agree to a recommendation by Mr. Justice Sloan to take away the statutory
Crowsnest rates. Well, Mr. Speaker, if that indicates the thinking of the government backbenchers, the farmers in western Canada certainly should be made aware of it so they can govern themselves accordingly.
We are opposing this legislation for fear it will prevent the introduction of the legislation that is needed. We object to the method of introduction by television programs. Evidently our friends in the Conservative party, who have objected to smaller things, take no objection to the fact that this program went on the air. We found that recently when a certain program did not go on the air, they joined us in protesting. We protest the failure of the government to accept the democratic representations of the farmers, and the failure of the government to follow the advice of farm organizations.
The threats and the intimidation levelled at the members of this party in particular by the Minister of Trade and Commerce are an indication of how right we are in opposing this measure. The minister has tried to deceive us in the same way one might try to deceive a small child into thinking that a bitter pill will be sweeter if followed by a bit of honey. The minister has told us we are not to be allowed to discuss the legislation relating to the payment of storage charges until we have swallowed this bitter pill. I think we are going to continue to discuss this until, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) pointed out, we can get some indication the government is prepared to take the action desired by the farmers.
There are various other arguments I could use to support my contention that this proposed legislation, as indicated by the title of the bill, is nothing but a farce. It is deceitful all the way through. I am hoping that by debating the issue we might be able to open some of the wilfully blind eyes of the members of the government. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North:
That Bill No. 82 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.

I understand the C.C.F. say "hear, hear" to that. I am going to read something that I think will carry conviction to every hon. member in this house except those who absolutely refuse to accept facts no matter how plainly proved. I hold in my hand a document entitled "The submission to the government of Canada respecting the urgent need for cash advances on farm-stored grain in western Canada." It is dated October 11, 1955, and was presented by: The Alberta department of agriculture; Manitoba department of agriculture; Saskatchewan department of agriculture; Saskatchewan wheat pool; Manitoba farmers' union; United Grain Growers; Saskatchewan federation of agriculture; Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation; Alberta federation of agriculture; Saskatchewan farmers' union; interprovincial farm union council; Alberta farmers' union.
I shall read from this submission, Mr. Speaker. Here is what it had to say in dealing with the marketing conference in Saskatoon. Pursuant to the resolution passed at that marketing conference, a committee representing that conference met the government to make this submission and here is what they presented. I am reading from page 5 of the submission:
While the long-term agricultural problems also received consideration the immediate problem of cash shortage held the spotlight at the conference and resulted in the following resolution being passed:
"Be it resolved that the organizations participating in this conference urge the government of Canada to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on grain in store on the farm and further that these advances should be up to one-half the value of the normal delivery expected and should be repayable on the basis of one-half of the value of each delivery made by the farmer."
The submission goes on to say:
While the principle of cash advances on farm-stored grain was unanimously endorsed by the organizations present at the conference various proposals were offered on the mechanics of making these advances. Proposals offered included a financing arrangement through the Canadian wheat board; financing through the banks; financing through a separate agency to be established for this purpose; and a proposal was made that the rural municipalities be used as a means of making the cash advances.

Opinions varied on the rate of interest to be charged the farmers, ranging from interest-free loans to a rate of 3 per cent. But all were agreed that existing commercial interest rates were excessive.
This delegation as assembled at Ottawa, on October 10, 1S55, endorses the principle of advances on farm-stored grain and believes that it must be made a practical reality. We would strongly urge that these advances be made immediately and that the interest rate, if any, be kept at a minimum.

It is said that this bill provides short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces, but I submit that it does not do that. I know of several who have approached bank managers for loans but who were refused on the

That is true. I was going to say that politicians generally from Saskatchewan seem to be somewhat on the noisy side and not quite so subdued, shall I say, as their neighbours from Manitoba and obviously, judging from the remarks of my hon. friend from Medicine Hat, their neighbours from Alberta.
However, I was referring to another politician from Saskatchewan on the opposite side of the house, the hon. member for Rosthern, who indicated that there was some difference of opinion between the provincial Conservative group and the federal Conservative group on this matter of providing cash assistance to farmers at the present time. He quoted from a newspaper account to the effect that the leader of the opposition in the Manitoba legislature called for cash payments rather than cash advances. Well, that is a newspaper report, and obviously the attempt to drive a wedge between two political groups is the technique of splitting hairs. I do not know whether I am allowed to do so, but I have the verbatim report of the speech by the leader of the opposition in the Manitoba legislature, and the wording in that speech quite specifically refers to cash advances to farmers with grain in storage on the farms. I would suggest that this verbatim report is much more accurate than any newspaper report of what he said could actually be.
Furthermore, on that score, not only is the opposition in the Manitoba legislature in favour of the cash advances scheme, but also the throne speech delivered in the legislature came out very strongly on behalf of the principle of cash advances in preference to the method proposed in the bill now before us as it has been enunciated by several members, an act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain."
I would submit that in principle this measure falls short of meeting the situation on two fundamental points. First of all, as I understand the situation in the west, and as it seems the majority of other members understand the situation, this is not what the prairie grain farmers have been requesting. They have invariably requested the cash advances principle. Not only have they as individual farmers maintained this unswerving viewpoint, but also their organizations and the provincial legislatures-so far as I know, the provincial governments-have also asked for the same principle. So, in view of those

Grain
circumstances, it is past understanding why this bill is before us at the present time. It is going directly in the face of the requests of the prairie grain farmers.
The other point I wish to emphasize is that it does not take care of the problem existing in the west at the present time. It does not do what it says it is going to do, that is, provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain. The phrase I should like to emphasize is "temporary financial difficulties". I feel that the use of that phrase is indicative of the fact that the government has failed completely to understand the nature of the economic problem that exists in our grain growing economy at the present time. I would suggest that not only does this measure not deal adequately with the immediate shortage of cash on the prairie farms but also it fails to take into consideration the fact that this is a long-term problem that arises from fundamental changes in the Canadian economy and also in the world economy itself.
On this point I should like to submit, Mr. Speaker, that in recent years Canada has been producing more and more grain. The suggestion is put forward that this is merely a temporary situation and that at any time the situation will reverse itself in the event of a drought or unfavourable conditions. That of course begs the question because at the moment the situation is-it has been so for the past decade or more-that the prairie region is producing more and more grain, more and more wheat on approximately the same acreage. At the same time, unfortunately, Canada's over-all proportionate share of the export market has been declining. For years we had 30 per cent of the total export market for wheat. We have hardly been holding that percentage notwithstanding the fact that the total world demand for wheat has been growing during recent years.
The bill before us refers to a temporary financial difficulty. I suggest that the financial difficulty is not a temporary one but is a problem that will continue for some years into the future until such time as the government moves to deal adequately with the changed circumstances in which Canada finds itself in relation to world markets. The wheat grower is dependent upon the export market to dispose of his crop, and the difficulty becomes more acute when he is in a position where he produces an abnormal amount of grain. Unfortunately the world market situation, instead of improving in the post-world war II climate, has been growing increasingly difficult.
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
Economic nationalism has been a factor of increasing prominence. We find that today our Canadian wheat trade operates within a jungle of import restrictions, milling prescriptions, tariffs, subsidies and the like which is the result of the growth of national policies in both import and export countries. If we are going to deal adequately with this so-called temporary financial difficulty, Canada must be placed in a position where she is competitive with other countries who are also participating in the export market for grain. Since the war we have attempted to deal with the problem by various international agreements, the international wheat agreement and also such United Nations organs as the food and agriculture organization. That approach to the problem is all to the good and should be encouraged.
It is becoming increasingly obvious, however, that, with the world situation now confronting us, we are not going to find any easy solutions to the problem of international trade. When the government suggests that the wheat board is not in a position to provide more adequately for the financial crisis of prairie wheat farmers, I think it is admitting that it is not willing to stand behind the wheat board. At the present time all other exporting countries, without exception, stand substantially behind the wheat producers in their particular countries. In Canada, however, the answer the government has given to the suggestion of the opposition that the present scheme of government-backed loans is inadequate and will not deal with the problem and that instead cash advances should be provided is to the effect that the wheat board is not in a position to provide such relief to the prairie farmers. That is suggesting that the government of Canada is not wining to stand behind the wheat board and give it the necessary support in order to deal adequately with the critical cash shortage of Canadian wheat growers at the moment.
I made the point before and I repeat that Canadian wheat growers are the only growers who are not assisted by their government in reaching a truly competitive situation in the world market. The wheat board, as it has been repeatedly pointed out, has no other moneys except those which it obtains from the sale of the farmers' wheat. Up until this year the farmer has been paying substantial amounts for storage charges, which has reduced his final payment. The government is moving to alleviate that to a certain extent through payment for excess grain in storage, but other than that the farmer has borne the total cost of handling his grain from his own money as realized from the

sale of grain by the Canadian wheat board ever since the board was established.
In carrying out this policy I say that the Canadian government is the only government that has placed the grain producer in this position. I do not have time to go into the details of the matter but it is obvious that there is a wheat war going on in the world. If we merely examine the attitude of our neighbour to the south we see that her position regarding wheat production has changed completely in the past few years. At one time she hardly produced enough for her own domestic consumption. I believe that prewar domestic consumption in that country was approximately 600 million bushels while production amounted to 700 million bushels so that her contribution to the world market was merely nominal. But now she has completely reversed that position and instead of producing 700 million bushels of grain she is producing up to 1 billion bushels and has occupied the position that Canada formerly occupied in the export market. I believe the emphasis on a temporary cash shortage and temporary financial difficulties falls far short of a realization of the actual situation. I believe it is five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

At five o'clock I was making the point that in the light of the steps taken to deal with the situation at the moment it is obvious the government does not fully appreciate the problem prevailing in our grain growing economy. I mentioned, as an example, the relative change in the position of Canada and the United States in the markets of the world. We must always remember that, in order to have a healthy
Grain
grain growing economy, Canada must constantly keep in mind that we are dependent upon the export market and must occupy a substantial percentage of that market. Unfortunately in recent years we have not even held our proportionate position, even though general world markets have been expanding since world war II.
I could continue to point out how other countries are attempting to deal with this problem because it is a problem that is not peculiar to Canada. Other major wheat growing countries have faced the same difficulty. Australia, for example, is deliberately curtailing the production of wheat and encouraging the farmers to move towards a diversified agricultural activity; that is a deliberate government policy. In this country government policy has not shown the same awareness of the difficulty and up to the present time, except for a few of the provincial governments, the federal administration has been encouraging maximum production of wheat and concentration on this one-product prairie farm economy. I feel that this points to the need for more substantial measures on the part of the federal government than the bill we have before us or any other legislation that has been introduced so far to deal with the situation.
I know the government reply to any suggestion of that kind is that the Canadian government is not in a position to offer any more encouragement or any more assistance to the prairie wheat producer because the wheat trade occupies such a large segment of the total Canadian economy that it would be completely impossible for the Canadian treasury to deal with this problem as have other countries throughout the world. This is true. But again, it comes back to the fact that nothing has been done by the Ottawa authorities to try to arrive at a more balanced position in our prairie economy. In fact, I would suggest that government policies, instead of alleviating the problems of agriculture as a result of a one product, unstable economy, have only aggravated the difficulty down through the years.
There is one more point I should like to mention in connection with this matter and that is that the price of grain on the domestic market has occupied an unfavourable position in relation to the cost of other consumer goods. If we were to examine the statistics for the past 18 years we would find that the prairie wheat grower has been subsidizing the consumer in Canada so far as the sale of his wheat is concerned. The price to the Canadian consumer has never corresponded, up until the last two years, to the price of wheat on the world market. For years it was pegged

Grain
at $1.25 to the Canadian miller when the price in the world market was soaring upwards to $2.83. It seems to me that the time has come when something has to be done by this government to bring the domestic price of wheat more closely into relationship with the general price level of other consumer goods.
In the past two years this problem has been brought to our attention with increasing force because the world wheat price has declined. As a result of the decline in world wheat prices, the prairie farmer finds himself in this cost-price squeeze about which we have heard so much during this session. When there is a surplus of a product, it is obvious that the price of that product is going to decline, and that is the position in which the grain producer finds himself. It is a position that has placed the whole prairie economy in serious jeopardy, because while the price of his product has been decreasing, unfortunately continued inflationary pressures, particularly in the industrial field, have resulted in the increased cost of producing his product.
From time to time hon. members from other parts of Canada complain that too much time is consumed in this house discussing the problem of wheat. I should like to suggest that until the government moves to do something more adequate than we have in this bill, hon. members are going to be forced to hear a lot more than they have heard in the past. There is a real problem in our grain growing economy and nothing that has been forthcoming from the government by way of legislative measures has even begun to deal with the difficulty. It is because of that that I can support, without any reservation, the amendment that has been moved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principal feature involved in this discussion to ratify legislation guaranteeing bank loans made to grain producers
Grain *
in the prairie provinces who face financial difficulties as a consequence of the government's inability to market prairie wheat appears to be twofold. The first is the inadequacy of this measure to answer the farmer's problems. The second is the various submissions that have been made from the opposition side of the house. We believe that in making those submissions we have consistently represented the opinions of the farmers of western Canada. I think the answer is to be found in cash on the line rather than in loans at the bank as a means of alleviating the problem which faces farmers at this time.
I rise to take part briefly in this debate because one does not necessarily have to be a farmer to understand the predicament in which farmers find themselves, and also because I believe the problem has been handled rather lightly by the government. It so happens that I represent an urban riding, but we in that riding know that our wellbeing depends upon the prosperity of the farmer. Furthermore, in my riding there are many retired farmers who still possess their investments in the farms, and their children are managing those farms. As a consequence I believe that they would want me to rise in my place at this time and express their feelings on this matter. I fully agree that this legislation in no way answers the need of farmers for a stable and adequate income. Clearly the answer is to have a policy and a platform which will ensure a stable and adequate income for the farmers. The government has no such policy. Such being the case, this legislation, which mskes lending facilities more readily available to the farmer, does help to improve his condition, but it must be considered as only a supplementary and additional measure. But let me make it perfectly clear that the farmers of western Canada are not satisfied merely with having the opportunity of borrowing money at banks. The farmers of western Canada are afraid of debt. They know from past experience, during the depression years, that there is only one thing worse than having a debt and that is having no markets, no money, and having a debt on top of that.
What is it that the farmer really wants? It seems to me that the farmer wants a solution to perhaps the most paradoxical problem of this age; namely the removal of his poverty in the midst of the plenty that he has made. I think the position of the farmer is very clear. He wants a policy and a platform that would first give encouragement and inducement for him to continue

' Grain
producing without being penalized for it, and secondly he wants a fair return for such an effort.
There are over 250,000 farm units in western Canada who have no way of expressing their feelings with respect to this legislation unless we in the opposition set them forth and indicate to the house the feeling of injustice that must overtake them when they see that we are asked to consider these bank loans in place of the legislation they asked for.
There is another point to which I should like to draw the attention of the minister and that is the high interest charges that are being made. With the government guaranteeing to chartered banks the loans they make to farmers, it seems to me that the element of risk or loss is completely removed from such bank loans. My point is that the farmers should not have to suffer the consequences of a situation for which they are not responsible; loss of markets, increased cost of production resulting from a jungle of taxation and the inability of the government to provide policies making saleable the farm production of wheat. It surely is not unreasonable to expect that banks, which are protected against loss, should also make a small concession and accept slightly less profit thereby helping to shoulder the burden which faces an important segment of our population. I hope the government will consider the advisability of so advising the banks.
I think we should get one thing straight and that is that the farmers of western Canada are not asking for charity or handouts. What they are asking for are measures that will make it possible for them to exchange their production for purchasing power. I think that is the only answer they are willing to accept. I think it is a reasonable request both in theory and in practice. In the United States of America the commodity credit corporation which was set up there does make prepayments and cash advances on wheat that is properly stored on farms. Furthermore, I believe that the entire debate thus far raises a theme that has not been mentioned, namely what should be done about the tremendous stockpiles of our surplus wheat?
Clearly the answer is not in cutting down production but in making consumption here and abroad more available. What is this government for if not to devise policies that will make this possible? As long as there are hungry people in the world, and indeed as long as there are people in this country who do not have enough to eat, we in this group
[Mr. Holowach.l
will certainly oppose any measure or suggestion that we plant trees or grass on those pieces of land which should quite rightly be producing crops.
The government is insisting that it receive gold or dollars for its surpluses in the matter of export. That is perfectly all right; let them proceed with an aggressive policy to acquire such payments for exports, but since they cannot receive gold or dollars for our surplus wheat, what is all this nonsense about our not accepting foreign currencies and not engaging in barter? Quite frankly I am glad that the farmers are demanding cash payments for their wheat.
They are asking in effect for income in return for having created real wealth, wheat. They are asking for purchasing power to equate their production power. I only hope that in asking for this they clearly understand that what they are asking for is the implementation of the monetary policies of social credit. I believe sincerely, that governments will have to implement these social credit policies sooner or later; there is no other way. My hope is that in making such demands the farmers understand that in reality they are asking for the implementation of fiscal policies and usage of the national credit of our country in order for them to obtain cash and not bank credit as is presently being advanced by this legislation.

Indeed, all of this discussion has merely postponed the next measure to come before us which will probably be Bill No. 83 which does attempt to and will provide a part of a long term policy.
I do not see the point of a great deal of the discussion which has wandered all over the field of international marketing and international finance and has dealt with all the difficulties with which farmers have been beset ever since the profession of farming existed and which will beset farmers for some
