I entirely agree with what the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) brought forward this afternoon with respect to the responsibility of the government in dealing with the situation following representations from responsible farm organizations as representatives of the Saskatoon conference. I am aware of what took place at that conference because I was there as an observer and I listened to all the discussion. If we merely try to shove this particular bill before the agricultural committee its passing will be postponed for some months.
If the undertaking is made, surely to goodness we are businessmen enough in this house -if not we should be-to look at Bill No. 82 for what it actually is. It is not a bill to deal with long-term agricultural policies. All of the discussion that is going on is simply holding up our proceedings, and that in the long run will hold up the final payment which will be made subsequent to the passing of Bill No. 83. Do not let anyone say that Bill No. 82 is deliberately placed where it is before Bill No. 83 which deals with storage and interest charged. I am getting just a little bit tired of all this finagling around all over the field of general farm policies when this has nothing to do with the question of a general farm policy. I am going to vote for this bill because it deals with a specific problem and makes a specific undertaking.

I believe that there is growing up in this country a doctrine which should be called the C. D. Howe doctrine. This doctrine entails subservience to ministerial undertakings. On the introduction of this bill we had the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stating to the public and to the banks that this government would undertake to spend public moneys through the undertaking of a minister, instead of waiting to call parliament together or to have the undertaking for the payment of public money made through the

proper channels. Instead of doing that the Minister of Trade and Commerce takes it upon himself to make this announcement at a public meeting.
After a very short period of debate in this house the right hon. minister had the audacity to get up and say that he was tired of the debate, that his patience was running out. He made the veiled threat-it was not so very veiled either-to the house that he was prepared to withdraw the legislation if hon. members continued to oppose it.
That was nothing short of a disregard for parliamentary procedure, for the integrity of this house. We should have in Canada supremacy of parliament, and veiled threats or intimidations should not be contained in any statement made by a minister in the house. In addition to that, the other day the right hon. minister stated that in illustrating the position of the western farmer I was more or less saying that the farmer was a man with a tin cup looking for a handout. That could not be further from the truth because the farmer in western Canada, and indeed in any part of the country, is not asking for a handout. The farmer is simply asking for justice, for some sort of equality of treatment.
The western farmers simply want to share in the prosperity that they see existing in this country. I feel that the time has come when we should not hear any more threats from the ministerial benches in this House of Commons. We should treat the subject before us in a parliamentary manner.
At the time the minister was taking such strong exception to the debate in this house he said quite incorrectly that the same speeches had been made more than twice by members from the prairies and then said that he saw a member getting up to speak for the third time. Nothing could be further from the truth because at that time the members of this group and indeed the members in all sections of the house had not spoken more than once on the subject. Whether the minister is happy about this legislation or not, the fact is that some of us are strongly opposed to it. We have given notice that we are going to oppose it in every way we can. It is now suggested that the bill be sent to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization where it can be examined and where perhaps some measure of progress can be made toward making it more acceptable to the western farmer. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) suggests that it be thrown into the wastepaper basket.
In order to deal with this subject properly I think we must examine the reason for the government wishing to bring in a measure of
(Mr. McCullough (Moose Mountain).]
assistance, if this can be called assistance. I think in order to do that we have to examine the condition of the farmers concerned. We have had on many occasions during the past few months explanations in the press for the condition of the western farmer.
I feel that the western farmer now is in one of the worst financial positions he has ever found himself in. The question is one of income. The farmer in western Canada, on the average, has a great deal of grain on hand and, indeed, he has been progressive in his methods of farming and has produced a great deal of livestock and other farm commodities. But the fact remains that the farmer's income in western Canada has fallen very drastically in the last three years, so seriously that he is now in a cost-price squeeze, so that he must have some assistance if he is going to be able to carry on.
I wish to point out at this moment that there has never been so much confusion, in respect to government policies pertinent to agriculture, as we see at this time. I was most amazed, just prior to coming back to parliament, that the press reported that, in addition to terminal storage at the coast ports and at the main terminal storage points, there were facilities for storing 58 million bushels of wheat and, in addition, in the other country elevators there was an additional storage space of over 44 million bushels. In other words, we were told there was storage available for over 100 million bushels of wheat. Yet up to that point the minister had been going to Washington and proclaiming to the press that it was the United States give-away policy in respect to wheat that was undermining the Canadian wheat sales.
On top of that, to show government mismanagement, while this storage space was available there were over 11,000 box cars absent from the prairies in the United States over and above the number of box cars from the United States in Canada. When it is considered that the western farmer must have the possibility of delivering his grain in many cases when the roads are open, it will be seen that the situation developing is one whereby the farmer in the middle of winter is unable to deliver his grain, regardless of whether or not there is an opening at the elevator. Here we have a lack of planning by the federal government. When we ask for some planning, they say, "You people think only of planning." This is one time when we could have had a little planning and where the transport commissioner must be sharply criticized for his inaction in not seeing to it that there were sufficient box cars to meet the situation prevailing at that time.

Now I should like to deal rather briefly with some of the aspects of farm income because I think it has a bearing on what we are trying to do at the present time. We in the C.C.F. group feel that this measure does not meet the needs of the western farmers. It is not only a short-term credit policy that we need, but I want to maintain that, if we had proper policies in this country to maintain the income of farmers, we would not now have to be dealing with a short-term credit proposal for western farmers such as proposed. While it is recognized that the general income of people throughout Canada has increased, it is still true that agriculture, even on a national basis, has deteriorated in the past three years.

The minister seems to think we are prepared to accept that method of doing the nation's business. I think not. I should like to point out to the minister that we might be in a better position on this bill had he made use of the resolution stage as it was intended to be used. The purpose of the resolution stage is to explain the nature of the legislation, to have debate and discussion as to the need for the legislation and hear suggestions from the minister concerning the contents of the bill with full disclosure of the details, giving an opportunity to revise the bill or withdraw it completely.
During the resolution stage of this bill a full debate was carried out. The minister was advised it was an unsatisfactory piece of legislation. He should have either made revisions in the bill before presenting it to us or withdraw it entirely. I should like to direct the attention of the house to what was done by Disraeli in 1867 when he was trying to introduce a contentious measure on reform in England. He did it by way of resolution. The resolution was debated vigorously and there was a great deal of opposition. As W. I. Jennings points out in his book on parliament, page 243, speaking of Disraeli he says:

Grain
come here again asking parliament to be a rubber stamp for something he has done beforehand. There is a great deal of objection here, and I hope elsewhere, to treating parliament in that fashion.
Earlier today the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) dealt with the meaning of the term "cash advances", and he attempted to show-he did it very badly-some change had been made in our position and that we were now talking about cash payments instead ofi cash advances. We had a great play on words with regard to what you mean by an advance. I gather that one of the leading papers in western Canada got mixed up in this too, by inadvertence. I was sorry to hear the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) apparently had also become confused with regard to the word "advances". He is usually quite well informed on the meaning of words.
In order to show that there has been no change in our position from quite early, let me draw to your attention the fact that on October 26, before this house assembled and when the crisis in the wheat situation was evident, the Leader of the Opposition spoke on the matter and is reported in the Ottawa Citizen of that date as follows:
He urged an immediate cash purchase plan by the wheat board of farm-stored western grain on a quota basis, making an initial payment thereon as if the wheat had been delivered to the elevators.
Later in this house the Leader of the Opposition used practically those very words and made it quite clear to everybody who was really interested in the matter that a payment was what was intended by the use of the word "advance", and it was clear to everyone except those who apparently did not wish to understand. He used such words as these, as reported at page 41 of Hansard:
Provision should be made for immediate cash advances in the ordinary way on the quota book by the wheat board for farm-stored grain on a quota basis, making an initial payment thereon as if the wheat had been delivered to the elevator.
And then, to make it doubly clear, he drew the attention of the house to that once again on Friday, January 27. There has been no change in the position of this party with regard to cash advances being intended to be a payment on grain, and being intended to be paid for by the delivery of that grain when it could be called forward. At the same time the Leader of the Opposition very properly urged in October, or thereabouts, that a special session be called. He urged earlier that a special session should be called to deal with the problem.

The foreword to the bill that has been placed before us reads:
An act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
I looked at this with some amazement, particularly the last phrase:	"inability to
deliver all their grain". The grain producers are apparently unable to deliver all their grain. They are ready, willing and able to do it. The fault lies elsewhere. The latter phrase of the bill should read: "arising from the failure of the policy of the government in respect of promoting the sale of wheat and in its failure to provide elevator space and box cars for delivery." It is not the fault of the grain producers; it is not their inablity to deliver their produce to the elevator.
The factors that have made this bill unsatisfactory are perfectly clear. They deserve full consideration. In order to indicate the unsatisfactory nature of this particular legislation hon. members who have spoken have dealt with all aspects of agriculture in relation to the wheat-growing problem and the marketing of wheat, and there is some sense to that type of approach, because unless you see this particular problem in relation to the whole it might not be easy to understand the opposition to this measure. This is an emergency measure. It apparently is filling a need only for a small number of grain producers. It is clear from what is expected or asked for by those who are spending their lives in the production of grain on the western plains. The situation has been drawn to our attention, but there is no harm in having a look at it again.
The situation of western agriculture in relation to agriculture as a whole is much worse from the standpoint of over-all loss of farm income in that part of the country than anywhere else in Canada, and we recognize that agriculture throughout Canada is in a difficult situation. The figures in the returns to the farm people of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta amount to a decrease of $404 million for 1954, and the situation is certainly not improving. When you are dealing With figures of that magnitude, surely it is an emergency that deserves consideration from Canada as a whole. That is a serious loss of income to western Canada, and indirectly to other parts of Canada.
The population of western Canada is rapidly approaching the 3 million mark. We are closely linked with all the provinces through agriculture. It was agriculture that brought about the development of the west and although in recent years we are having

the good fortune to discover oil and to develop mining industries and to develop and use our forest products, nevertheless agriculture has been and still is basic to the welfare of western Canada, and affects a very large proportion of Canada's population. Then we all know that the income resulting from the sale of our wheat has certainly been very beneficial to those engaged in industry in other parts of Canada. Of course it has affected the whole transportation system of our country, which in western Canada was certainly developed on the basis of the export of wheat, and it has certainly affected the Atlantic and Pacific ports that handle our grain, and generally it has been of great importance to the whole economy of Canada.
Now, when you consider the decrease in the income of western Canada, because of the inability of the government to market our wheat and to pay farmers for what they have produced, you can see that the effect is widespread, and that Bill No. 82 does not deal with the problem except in a very minor way. It will not put into the hands of the farmers of western Canada the cash they need at the present time to pay their general expenses and to make preparations and provisions for the new crop year of 1956, which is fairly close at hand.
We have been informed that the loans are still limited in principal and in quantity, and that means of course that the shortage of cash still exists. It is incumbent upon all of us to speak out on this measure not simply because we may come from western Canada but because of our interest in the development of agriculture as a whole in this country. If western agriculture suffers very severely, as it is suffering at the present time, the effect is bound to be felt elsewhere. It may be a delayed effect, but it is a type of creeping paralysis which will gradually affect other parts of the country.
The proposal has been made that this bill, instead of being proceeded with forthwith, be referred to the agriculture committee for study. There is sense to that suggestion, because here in the house the minister has brushed aside some of the suggestions that have been made; whereas in committee they might be more carefully considered, and the whole implication of this bill and its effect on western agriculture given the closest attention.
The committee might well relate the wheat problem to our export markets and look ahead a bit in regard to our future policy in respect of wheat. It was just by chance that the short crop of 1954 staved off this problem for a year. That short crop aided the government in avoiding the issue with regard to the problem of disposing of our
Grain
wheat. Well, it caught up to them in 1955 because the crop was good and now with the carry-over that faces us for 1956 the problem is going to be with us throughout the fall of 1956 and 1957. This bill may be extended, of course, to cover 1957 but as it is ineffective right now it will be ineffective in 1957 as well.
Throughout this debate and despite meetings of farm organizations and representations by letter and by telegram to the members of the government, absolutely no regard seems to have been paid to the opinion of the western farmer. Perhaps I should not put it that broadly but certainly not sufficient regard has been paid to that opinion. It has been brushed aside. That strikes me as peculiar because there are no sounder people than those engaged in agriculture in the western provinces. As all farmers are, they are sensible people who look at their problems pretty calmly and deliberately and they discuss and debate before they put forward their proposals. I have had an association with western farmers for over 50 years and I rank them as among the most sensible portion of our population.

And yet, in the face of their suggestions over the last several months, the minister has refused to consider the problem as the farmer of western Canada sees it. The farmer without cash is being carried along by his friend the village or town storekeeper. It is an intolerable situation, really, for a man who has produced a very valuable product,

Grain
Canada's wheat, which has for so many years been ranked as the most important wheat in the World. The man who produces wealth of that nature and adds to the gross national product is now told to wait for the government to dispose of his grain, to go and borrow money from a bank and pay 5 per cent interest on it and just hope for the best. I do not wonder at all that the farmers have been indignant about this method of dealing with their problem because it has struck close to home. They are the ones who know exactly what they need in order to manage from month to month and in order to pay their harvesting costs during the fall and to pay the normal costs of the winter and to get ready for spring. They naturally need cash and they have the security in this first-class wheat, which in this last crop year was of a higher quality than in some other years. On that basis surely the farmer has been right in asking for a method different from the one put forward by the minister.
Earlier in this debate I was disappointed to hear the minister suggest that perhaps the security was not good enough and that the farmers might dispose of their grain in some other way and would not be able to meet their obligations. That is not the western farmer as I have known him. The western farmer is prepared to meet his obligations on all occasions. The percentage of farmers who would not meet their responsibilities would not be any greater than in any other group; it would perhaps be one-half of one per cent. No, the farmer can be trusted and in this instance he should have been trusted and his advice should have been taken.
Why has there been this neglect of western Canada? What has happened to the government of this country that it can brush aside the expression of opinion from that great section of our country, the three prairie provinces with their large, active and thriving population, that section of Canada that has produced a great deal of wealth for this nation?
The representation of western Canada in the House of Commons, as we know, is divided. It shows the interest and activity and political alertness of western Canadians. It reveals that they do not simply follow along behind the government of the day. They are familiar with protesting when things are not going right. They have protested in the past, and very effectively, but at this time with all that experience behind us surely we can see that the voice of the western farmer, expressed through his normal farm organizations, should be heard and listened to attentively by this government and the proposals

of the western farmer for cash advances, or for cash payments, which is the same thing, on farm-stored grain should have been accepted by this government long ere this. This bill should have been withdrawn between resolution stage and its presentation to this house, and it could now be withdrawn by the minister and altered to meet the circumstances of this particular period.
I think the government is neglecting western Canada and that this minister who caused us so much trouble last year is adopting the same attitude again this year. He wants to force this through parliament no matter how many sound organizations may be against putting it forward at this time. And that is the type of treatment of parliament against which we protest.
I urge the minister now-it is not too late- to withdraw the bill and bring in something really worth while.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the house is pleased to have a statement from the minister, particularly his statement that he felt that the legislation which they introduced last fall was a solution to the immediate problem. The minister refers to the discussion today as being a filibuster. That is not the first time that he has referred to a debate as being a filibuster. If he wants to have a filibuster, we will show him what a filibuster is, and that will completely block the legislation.
What we are doing here is expressing emphatically our opposition to the policy of this government to deal with what is a very critical situation, the cash shortage on the prairie provinces. The minister's statement that this is a solution to that problem shows how completely he misunderstands the problem and how uninformed he is as to the real situation.
It is the same kind of thing we have had in this house before during this session. We have heard talk about the great prosperity which Canada is enjoying from east to west, but then it was said that there are a few

people who are not enjoying this great prosperity to the full. One portion of Canada which is not enjoying fully this prosperity is the three prairie provinces.
That area of Canada is suffering an economic recession, because the farmers are unable to deliver their grain because of the policies of this government and its failure to sell wheat. Then when wheat was sold it has failed to fill the space in the elevators which was made available. They tell us that the box cars are away, that the transport controller is not available. The result is that the farmers are unable to get any cash from the delivery of grain, which is the basis of the economy in the west.
I shall use the figures placed on the record, and left on the record by the Minister of Agriculture last Friday afternoon. According to those figures of net farm income in the prairie provinces, whereas the net farm income in the maritimes dropped by about 19 per cent from 1952 to 1954, in the province of Quebec about three per cent, and in Ontario about 15 per cent, in Manitoba the drop was 54 per cent in net cash income, in Alberta it was 50 per cent, and in the province of Saskatchewan, where most of this objection is coming from, it was 77 per cent.
If the minister realized what that situation means to those people, he would not bring in this kind of legislation which forces the people who are put in this position by the policies of the government, to go to the banks and borrow money if they are able. There are certain very stringent regulations, and the bank managers have apparently been instructed to be very careful about their loaning, and the deductions which must be taken off any loan for which they may qualify in the way of taxation arrears, lien notes and other indebtedness, including any cash that they may have obtained from a small delivery of grain which they may have had. It is all very well for the minister, in talking about this debate, to refer to what he hears from this side of the house as "blather".

I suggest to him that what some hon. members say, such as the hon. member for Rosthern this afternoon, might be called blather by us. He was sent here by the people of Rosthern to represent them. He can make his charges that we are deliberately misrepresenting the case and make such statements as that, but surely the evidence is before the house, the evidence of those people who know the situation, when the wheat pools and farm organizations, the

people involved from the three western provinces, come down here and place the facts before the government.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has the bureau of statistics under his department and he knows the cash situation is serious. We are looking for a solution and we are trying to persuade this government there is something wrong. If we are repeating ourselves, it is only in an attempt to persuade the members opposite and the people of Canada that there is a serious situation and that this legislation does not solve it. That is why we are emphatic in our opposition.
We are opposed to this measure because we think it is wrong in principle. These people are forced into the serious economic condition they are in on the western prairies today by government policy. Apparently their crime is that they have produced too much and have had a good crop. Surely, when they have produced the crop-and they have difficulty in some years in doing so- they should be entitled to deliver it. They are asking the government to allow them to deliver it. Surely the government is responsible for their condition and should undertake the responsibility for easing the situation, by allowing them to have the same cash advance-in fact, it is only half of the cash advance-which the same farmers would have if the government had provided the means whereby they could have delivered the grain. That grain, instead of being in store in the elevators, will still be on the farm. It will still be entered in the farm's permit book and it will be held against any future deliveries. That the farmer should be burdened with another loan, with another note against his personal property and all his production and a note to the bank or to the mortgage company, is wrong. That is why the opposition is very emphatic. I know we are a minority group in this house, but the only way we have of letting the government know that the people out there are opposed to this legislation is by constantly repeating it and letting the government know that this is an injustice. It is our duty to oppose it and we intend to continue doing so.
I have always admired the way the hon. member for Rosthern tackles an impossible problem. We have had another great demonstration of that from him again this afternoon. He tried to persuade this house that because the Minister of Agriculture, from the province of Saskatchewan, was at a conference in Saskatoon where efforts were made to get the government to meet the situation adequately, he supported the conference decision to ask for advances and, because he supported that, therefore he
Grain
supported bank loans. That is an utterly ridiculous stand for any person to take. The people just do not accept it. I maintain that every one of the members who came down here to interview the cabinet and told them that they wanted cash advances for grain on the farm through the wheat board, was certainly very disgusted when they found that all they got was an arrangement through the banks, whereby a very small percentage of the people who would need it were going to be allowed to borrow money and have a lien on their backs and pay interest-another toll to the banks.
What is this government doing about it? They are being very beneficent in their attitude. They say, "We are just going to guarantee that the banks will not lose any money. The banks will have to collect the loan when the grain is delivered. The banks will get the interest. We will see that the banks do not lose anything." I do not suppose this will cost the government anything. The last time they had similar legislation on the books, in 1952, their losses were almost negligible.
Because it fails completely to do the job that is needed desperately, we oppose it.
We also feel that perhaps Canada can afford to do something for these people. The government has to accept the responsibility for their condition and cannot get out of it. If the rest of Canada is enjoying tremendous prosperity, then I say that to condemn the prairie producers to this kind of condition, at a time like this when the remedy is so easy, is to discriminate against the people in that part of the country. That is the reason for the opposition, not only from members on this side of the house but from the people of that part of the country, in the representations that come to this government from the daily press and from the boards of trade and certainly, emphatically, in the representations from the farmers. I believe that the cabinet is going to receive another delegation from the interprovincial farm union, probably this week. I would suggest to them that again they look to the representations that come from that interprovincial farm union with regard to this legislation and see whether or not the legislation which is being brought into this house at this time is any kind of solution to the problem. The unanimous decisions of the mass protest meetings held across the country show that there is a great deal of dissatisfaction, and it is emphatic.
This Bill No. 82, now before us for second reading, is being discussed in principle. I have outlined the principles under which it operates. It is merely a bank loan. It is a system under which the farmer has to go to

Grain
the banks, and many farmers find it very difficult to get to the banks in our part of the country. I believe there are approximately 1,200 delivery points where the farmers haul their grain to the elevators, but there are less than 200 places, or one-sixth the number of delivery points, where there are any banks or lending institutions of the type that are allowed to lend money under this legislation. There are credit unions which the farmers use but the credit unions are told that their organization apparently is not suitable to carry on this kind of lending. They are not going to be included among those who can make loans which the government will guarantee.
It is wrong in principle to ask people, who find themselves placed in an uneconomic position by the actions of the government, to burden themselves with a further load of debt, but it seems very difficult to put that basic principle across in the house. We have repeated it and we have still to find anyone on the government side of the house who will say that the principle is sound and right. I will vote for the amendment and I want to compliment the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) on his attitude with respect to the bill. It is further evidence that people from the prairie provinces are disturbed about it. They recognize that it is wrong. They recognize that to support it is to support something which is wrong in principle and they refuse to do that.
Among the things that have disturbed western people as far as this measure is concerned is the fact that in the past they have had their hopes raised by statements made by ministers in the house. I can remember sitting here on several occasions last year, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) told us that the farmers would be able to deliver all the grain they had in store prior to the 1955 crop and that before the 1955 crop moved their bins would be empty. He raised their hopes but their hopes proved to be groundless. Some farmers have been allowed to deliver their eight bushel quota but many have not been able to do even that.
The minister referred to this measure as being a solution for all the problems of the farmer. It is very far from a solution so far as they are concerned. As a matter of fact, we have stressed for years that there is something basically wrong with an economic system under which the farmer has to operate with rising costs and decreasing returns. Even with the payments that have been made on the farmers' grain their income has been kept at a low level and agriculture is facing a very serious economic situation not only in western Canada but throughout the whole

country. The extra burden placed on the western farmer by this legislation is really a slap in his face. He sees that, not only is he facing bankruptcy with a continuation of the policies now in effect, but also that even with the delivery of his grain he is faced with the problem of decreased income from his farm and constantly increasing costs of operation.
The protests from the farmers are spontaneous. For the Minister of Trade and Commerce to try to mislead the house by saying that the demand for cash advances through the wheat board comes from the businessmen and from people wishing to destroy the wheat board is completely and utterly unfounded. The rank and file of the farmers have expressed their opposition through the only means they have, and that is where the opposition comes from. The dissatisfaction of the farmers with conditions is completely justified. The farmer rejects the offer of a further loan as being a rebuke to the western grain grower. He rejects the offer of the government to guarantee loans as an insult to his intelligence. He is trying to make the government appreciate that there is a real problem here that requires solution. We are opposed to the measure because it is impractical. We are opposed to it because it is completely ineffective in solving the problem, and the red tape involved in trying to get a loan is such that it will discourage the farmer in almost every instance.
Among the prairie people there is a sort of ingrown distrust of loans, notes, mortgages and the like. They have bitter memories of the results of going into debt when cash income is reduced and they are unable to cope with the situation. Thousands of farmers lost everything they had in the thirties when they were affected by the same situation, and it was a lesson they have never forgotten. They are opposed to mortgages and they dislike going into debt with the banks. They have had experience before with loans and they do not want any more. They also know that when in the past provincial governments attempted to save the farmer from foreclosure and the loss of everything he owned by passing legislation to protect the farmer and his wife and family on the home quarter, the Supreme Court of Canada declared such legislation was ultra vires of the provinces.
They find that in every case the money interests are protected and the protection of the farmer, his wife, his family and home is secondary. Apparently justice is always given first to the banker, to the sacred rights of money, capital and interest. The preference is always given to the money lender and the wife, the family and the home come second.

Court conflicts which have always ended in protecting the sacred rights of capital have made the people of the west very much opposed to any idea of loans and debt. I have known cases where the bread earner of the family lost his life through an accident and the wife and children were forcibly evicted on the road allowance in order to satisfy the rights of capital and the interest that had to be paid. Surely it is time that humanity came first and the rights of capital second.
The producer also knows that borrowing money does not solve any problem for him. It is no solution. It merely adds to his burden. Apparently the government is grimly determined not to consider the proposal for cash advances made by our party and the people from the prairies. There are almost 4,000 elevator agents in Saskatchewan as compared with less than 200 bank managers and if cash advances were made through the wheat board for grain properly stored on the farm the elevator agent, who has the producer's permit book, knows him personally and deals with him every year, could easily go to the farm, inspect the grain and see that is it properly stored and graded. If the government should require it, he could put a seal on it.
Let the farmer sign a document that he will not sell it except through his permit book, enter the advance in the permit book, and I can assure the government that they will be perfectly safe. Surely that is a fair and equitable method and a practical means of solving the problem. The bank loan legislation is absolutely useless in meeting the situation. We reject it and the people reject it. The determination of the government to force it through is going to be met by equal determination on the part of those of us who represent these people and are sent here to speak for them.

I should like to make it clear at the start that I do not believe the speakers from the opposition benches truly represent the thinking of the majority of wheat farmers in western Canada. The government proposes by this legislation

Grain
to guarantee bank loans to wheat producers in western Canada on farm-stored grain at 5 per cent interest with a ceiling of $1,500 on the loan. A little later we will also be discussing another bill which proposes that the government pay interest and storage charges on wheat held by the wheat board over the normal carry-over level. It is estimated this will cost the government $30 million.
While at the moment we are discussing the bill in connection with bank loans, yet I feel that both bills must be taken into consideration in order to fully appreciate the assistance being provided by the government to meet the emergency situation faced by western wheat producers. The position taken by the C.C.F. group and other opposition members is that the guaranteeing of bank loans up to $1,500 is not sufficient. As an alternative they suggest the wheat board should make cash advances on farm-stored grain. Some even say that these cash advances should be made without any interest being charged. I am afraid I cannot agree with hon. members opposite.
In the first place, the wheat board was established as a marketing agency and not a lending institution. The wheat board has neither the money nor the administration facilities to carry on such an extensive lending program. Even though the wheat board could borrow the necessary money at a lower interest rate than the farmers could get pn the same loan from the bank, the administrative costs would be far greater. The difference in the interest rates would not make up the cost of administration. Neither can I subscribe to any suggestion that the rest of Canada should pay the interest charges on these loans on farm-stored grain.
When a manufacturer over-produces in order to provide employment for his workers nobody underwrites the interest charges on his bank loans or provides him with interest-free capital. When an industrial worker is out of work and unable to meet his monthly payments on his home in which he has invested his life savings, he has to borrow money wherever he can at whatever interest rate is necessary in order to meet his obligations and save his equity and his home.
What is the present situation so far as the western wheat producer is concerned? During the past four years, with favourable climatic conditions, there have been bumper crops of wheat. The wheat board has exported more wheat in each of those years than they did in any of the post-war crop years from 1947 to 1951. This is also true for the crop year 1954-55. In spite of this there is still a considerable amount of wheat in storage on farms and in elevators. But according to the

dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin dated February 7 of this year, there is very little change in the visible supplies of wheat as compared with January 25 a year ago. The bureau's figures indicate that the visible supplies of Canadian wheat as of that date total 359,778,000 bushels as against 357,151,000 the year previous.
The position of the western wheat producer has not worsened, therefore, to any great extent in the past year. I appreciate the fact that he needs some help at the moment, and I intend to support this bill, which will enable wheat farmers who need financial assistance to get bank loans. I also intend to support the other bill when it comes before the house. This bill would allow the government to pay interest and storage charges on wheat held by the wheat board over and above the normal carry-over level. I intend to support these bills because I recognize it is impossible for Canada to maintain its present high level of prosperity unless all sections of the economy share in that prosperity or are assisted in some way.

As an hon. member pointed out the other day, we know your history. These younger members do not know it so well, but we know that you were the champions of free enterprise, of the Winnipeg grain exchange long ago, and now you are heralding in a loud voice that we are trying to destroy the wheat board. We created it; you have never supported it until the last few years and then you mongrelized it with all sorts of socialistic ideas that have nearly destroyed it. That is what has happened to the wheat board. Anything for political expediency.
This wheat situation today is not a greater problem than it was before. Today we produce only about 5-5 per cent of world production, but in the years when these tired old gentlemen you are talking about-a few years ago you said our party did not do anything to market wheat-we had twice as large a percentage of world production as you have now. We had 40 per cent of the world trade and in three years you cut it down to 18 per cent, and this year you have only 26 per cent. The United States of America exported only one-quarter as much wheat as we did before you came into power; since you came into power they are exporting almost twice as much as we are. We have a smaller proportion of the world production of wheat than we have had at any time since 1925.
These sales champions are trying to tell you now that they have done a great job, that nobody else could do as well. Nobody since confederation has made such a mess of things. Talk about changing policy. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce tells us that the United States of America is spoiling this. If it does not rain too much in the United States of America everything will be all right. You carry out a policy when you think everything will be all right.

Yes, nothing could be cheaper than the type of policy being carried on by these bread and butter twins that are trying to sell the products of Canada. One is smothered with wheat and the other is strangled with butter. One says that a billion bushels of wheat is not too much, that if it does not rain too much things will be all right and we can sell our wheat. The other twin says that they have only 100 million pounds of butter, that is not too much, the grass may be short next summer.
No wonder the farmers of Canada are dissatisfied. No wonder the young farmers of Canada are coming to members every weekend, as they come to me, wondering what they can do. Yet the right hon. Minister of Agriculture says that in Ontario they should not kick so much. You would think that they were expecting their adherents in the country to be as pliant as the Grit followers here. But they are befogged and bewildered and bitter. They do- not know what way to turn. They ask me, "What shall I do? Shall I put another mortgage on the farm or shall I quit and try to get a job at Malton?" They are saying up and down the sidelines and bylines that neither the Right Hon. Jimmy Gardiner nor the Right Hon. C. D. Howe knows what is going on. The parade has gone by them. They have been at Ottawa so long, they are too tired to listen, they are too smug to look.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly shall try to do that. I am glad that you suggested to me that you are going to allow me the same latitude as you allowed the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. White). We both will do our best to stick closely to the issue before the house. It is an important issue because it affects the economy of the whole dominion. The necessity for having either loans or cash advances has been brought about by the sales policy of the government. Probably you were not following me, but I was only trying to point out that one of the reasons was that a few years ago when I suggested to the right hon. Minister of Agriculture that we should not sell wheat for $400 million or $500 million less than the world wanted to pay for it, because the farmers might be able to use that money, he said to me, and the Speaker did not call him to order, "Don't you trust your English friends as I do?" I remember saying to him that I trusted them to be better traders than he , was. To use the slang of the streets, how the chickens are coming home to roost! How those British traders must laugh at these bread and butter twins who thought they knew how to sell our products.

We have lost our market in Britain. Talk about stabilizing the market. In those years Britain was supplying only about 23 per cent of her wheat requirements. Today she is supplying about 35 per cent of her wheat requirements. France was just about producing what she required; she exported over 90 million bushels last year. These are the people who told the world that they would sell wheat at X price and the world would have to pay for it. They have changed their tactics. We have lost those markets today. Now we find one of those honourable traders searching behind the iron curtain for markets for agricultural products, while we find the right hon. Minister of Agriculture flirting with the same people to get rid of our wheat. That is a country that produces a great amount of wheat, and China alongside it produces many times as much wheat as we do. The farmers have been told that they never had it so good. The people who have never had it so good are the elevator people of western Canada storing the wheat that this government has failed to sell. They are the people who have had it the best.
The government now proposes to say to these gentlemen, "You cannot sell your wheat anywhere else. Some of your wheat we trade pound for pound for hay in Alberta. We are going to investigate you through the grain commissioners to see how much wheat is being sold in mixed grains to the United States. Now we are going to say that you cannot sell it to anybody else. If you have a farm in Alberta and live in Saskatchewan, you cannot feed it to your steers in Alberta". Look at this cabinet; they cannot eat it. They have the wheat situation in Canada in the most colossal muddle it has been in since confederation. They are condemning everybody else. They try to say that we destroyed the wheat board. We gave it its birth. They would not even accept the child on their doorsteps for the first four years. They owned it only after they had mongrelized it, as I have said. They have put political expediency on every term in the wheat pools and socialized agriculture to the extent that the farmers of Canada do not know where they are going. The dairymen of Canada are dissatisfied. The potato growers in the east are dissatisfied. The fruit and vegetable growers in my district are dissatisfied. The wheat growers of western Canada are dissatisfied. Tonight they say, "After we have made all these plans, you will pay 5 per cent for what any member of the cabinet can borrow at 4J per cent. You will get the money at 5 per cent provided you have good credit".

In this whole issue, I am not concerned as to whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce withdraws the bill or threatens parliament or says, "We will not give these farmers anything until next July." There are 200,000 producers in western Canada, and in the first two weeks when this was brought in only 3,000 accepted the advances. The great bulk of those farmers out there borrowed in the same way as we farmers in Ontario borrowed. They paid their five per cent or whatever their credit would warrant in the banks. If all those who require it hound around through western Canada and find the branch banks and get acquainted with the bank managers, probably only about 5,000 or 6,000 out of the 200,000 will take advantage of it. So I might say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he may accept parliament or he may threaten parliament that he will do this or that if 3,000 or 4,000 more of the farmers of western Canada do not get a loan out of the 200,000. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce says he will close the door, he is all excited about nothing and out of breath for no purpose.
The trouble is that we have not performed as good salesmen. Surely the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce will admit at long last that they have failed as salesmen of our agricultural products. I have great regard for both of them. Their political nimbleness has been astounding to all those who have not understood what was going on. They have gained the admiration, the applause and the desk-thumping of all their silent supporters in the back benches, many of whom are much brighter than they, in the last few years, but the farmers of Canada know very well that these men who have posed as champion salesmen, if it were not for the taxpayers' money, would have gone bankrupt long ago in selling Canada's products. In the last two or three years the Minister of Agriculture has allowed the dairy industry to be invaded by oleomargarine, and the other night he used oleomargarine himself.
It is a spectacle such as I have not seen since I have been in parliament, and I am not surprised that the farmers today are dissatisfied. I am not surprised that the young farmers have lost hope. I am not surprised that the old farmers are worried, because they find their government so complacent, smug and inconsiderate as to say that the farmers of Ontario are kicking too much and have nothing to kick about. The farmers in western Canada-the wheat growers- have something to kick about. I have every sympathy with the wheat growers of western
